title: Our ears: how we hear, how to protect hearing, and the sounds animals hear that we can't

summary.text: A phone can be playing music while you hear nothing at all. Every ear has a quietest sound it can catch, and softer sounds pass it by. Your ear works as a chain. The ear flap collects sound, the eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones pass the vibration on, and hair cells in the cochlea turn it into signals for the brain. People hear only a band of pitches, and the top of that band drops as we grow older. Loud sound can break hair cells, and in people they never grow back, so ears need protecting. Bats, moths, cats and dogs hear sounds too high for us, and elephants and pigeons hear sounds too low for us. Each of them hears what their own life needs.
summary.art: A child with eyes shut and one hand raised, listening to a phone across the room. Around the room, faint coloured sound lines that the child cannot hear: a bat at the window, a cat with ears turned, and an elephant's low rumble drawn as long slow waves.

intro.hook: Try this. Play a song on a phone and turn the volume all the way down, but leave the song playing. Put the phone on a table across the room. Can you hear it? The song is playing, and the phone is sending out sound. So why can't you hear it?
intro.text: Your ears catch only sounds that are loud enough, and only sounds of certain pitches. In this unit you find the quietest sound you can hear, and you test which ear covers block sound best. You follow a sound from your ear flap to your brain. You find out why very loud sounds can harm hearing for ever, and how to keep your ears safe. You also meet animals that hear sounds we never notice: bats, moths, elephants and more.
intro.art: A phone lying on a table across a room with its music app open and the volume bar at zero, and a girl on the far side cupping a hand behind her ear, looking puzzled.

outcomes: I can follow a sound through my ear: ear flap, ear canal, eardrum, three tiny bones, cochlea, hair cells, nerve and brain.
I can find the quietest sound I can hear, and test fairly which ear cover blocks the most sound.
I can explain why loud sound can harm hearing for ever, and name ways to protect my ears.
I can say why nothing should go into the ear canal, and what earwax does.
I can name animals that hear sounds too high or too low for people, and say how that hearing helps their lives.
I can explain that pitch depends on how fast something vibrates, and that people hear only a band of pitches that gets narrower with age.

terms.meaning: The curved part of the ear on the outside of your head. It collects sound and sends it into the ear hole. Its scientific name is the pinna.
terms.example: Cup your hand behind your ear flap, and a fan's hum sounds louder, because you collect more sound.
terms.art: A child's ear seen from the side, with the curved ear flap shaded and an arrow showing sound going into the ear hole.

terms.meaning: The short tube from the ear hole to the eardrum. In a grown-up it is about 2.5 cm long.
terms.example: Earwax is made in the walls of the ear canal.
terms.art: A cut-away of the ear showing a short tube leading from the ear hole inwards to a thin round skin.

terms.meaning: A thin, tight skin at the end of the ear canal. It vibrates when sound reaches it, like the skin of a tabla.
terms.example: When someone claps, the vibrating air makes your eardrum vibrate too.
terms.art: A round thin skin at the end of a tube, with small curved lines showing it vibrating.

terms.meaning: To move quickly back and forth. Every sound starts with something vibrating.
terms.example: A veena string vibrates when it is plucked, and so does your eardrum when the sound reaches you.
terms.art: A plucked veena string drawn blurred, moving back and forth.

terms.meaning: Three tiny bones behind the eardrum, called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. They pass the vibration from the eardrum to the cochlea. The stirrup is the smallest bone in your body.
terms.example: The stirrup is about 3 millimetres long, smaller than a grain of rice.
terms.art: Three tiny linked bones, shaped like a hammer, an anvil and a stirrup, next to a grain of rice for size.

terms.meaning: A tube coiled like a snail shell, deep inside your head. It is filled with liquid and lined with hair cells.
terms.example: The cochlea is about the size of a pea.
terms.art: A snail-shaped coil next to a green pea of the same size.

terms.meaning: A cell in the cochlea with a tiny tuft on top. When sound makes the tuft bend, the cell sends a signal along a nerve. Each ear has about 15,000 of them.
terms.example: Different hair cells pick up high sounds and low sounds.
terms.art: A close-up of a row of cells, each with a tuft of tiny stiff hairs on top, bending as a ripple passes.

terms.meaning: The nerve that carries signals from the hair cells to the brain. Auditory means to do with hearing.
terms.example: The brain gets signals along the auditory nerve and you hear the pressure cooker whistle.
terms.art: A thin cord running from the snail-shaped cochlea to the brain, with small sparks travelling along it.

terms.meaning: A soft, sticky yellow-brown substance made in the ear canal. It traps dust and tiny insects, and slowly moves out of the ear on its own.
terms.example: A little earwax at the ear hole is normal and healthy. It is not dirt.
terms.art: A cut-away ear canal with a thin layer of wax on its walls and a speck of dust stuck in it.

terms.meaning: How high or low a sound is. A thing that vibrates faster makes a higher pitch.
terms.example: A koel's call has a high pitch. A big drum has a low pitch.
terms.art: A small bird singing with tightly packed sound lines beside a big drum with widely spaced sound lines.

terms.meaning: The unit for counting vibrations each second. 1 hertz is one vibration in one second.
terms.example: A young child can hear from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz.
terms.art: A clock with a second hand and a string vibrating beside it, with tally marks counting the vibrations.

terms.meaning: Sound with a pitch too high for people to hear, above about 20,000 hertz.
terms.example: Many bats hunt with ultrasound calls.
terms.art: A bat flying at night with tight wavy lines coming from the mouth, and a child below hearing nothing.

terms.meaning: Sound with a pitch too low for people to hear, below about 20 hertz.
terms.example: The lowest part of an elephant's rumble is infrasound.
terms.art: An elephant with long, slow, wide wavy lines spreading out across the grass.

terms.meaning: The softest sound that your ears can just catch. Scientists call it your hearing threshold. A sound softer than this reaches you, but you do not hear it.
terms.example: In the volume test, Kavya heard the song first at volume step 3. Step 3 was her quietest sound at that distance.
terms.art: A volume bar on a phone with the first few steps grey and a bright mark at step 3 where the girl raises her hand.

terms.meaning: The unit for measuring how loud a sound is. A whisper is about 30 decibels. A mixer grinder is about 80 to 90 decibels.
terms.example: Sounds above about 85 decibels, heard for a long time, can harm hearing.
terms.art: A ladder of sounds from bottom to top: a whisper, people talking, a mixer grinder, a traffic horn, a firecracker.

terms.meaning: When a person hears less than before, in one or both ears. It can come from age, illness or loud sound.
terms.example: Many grandparents find it harder to hear high sounds, like the 's' in words.
terms.art: A grandfather leaning towards a girl who is speaking clearly, facing him.

terms.meaning: A trained person who tests hearing and helps people who hear less.
terms.example: An audiologist plays soft beeps through headphones and asks you to raise your hand at each one.
terms.art: A woman audiologist with a laptop, and a boy in headphones raising his hand.

terms.meaning: Hearing through the bones of your head. The bones carry vibrations straight to the cochlea.
terms.example: When you hum with your ears shut, the hum sounds louder, because it reaches you through your bones.
terms.art: A child humming with fingers over the ear flaps, with wavy lines passing through the skull to the inner ear.

terms.meaning: Finding things by making a sound and listening to the echo that bounces back. An echo is a sound that bounces off something and comes back.
terms.example: Bats and dolphins find their food by echolocation.
terms.art: A bat sending out curved sound lines that bounce off a moth and come back.

explanations.concept: How the ear turns a sound into a signal
explanations.definition: Sound is a vibration of the air. The ear passes the vibration inwards from the eardrum to the cochlea, and hair cells there turn it into nerve signals for the brain.
explanations.description: When a bell rings, it vibrates, and the air around it vibrates too. Your ear flap collects some of that vibrating air and sends it down the ear canal. At the end, the eardrum vibrates. The three tiny bones pass the vibration on to the cochlea. The bones make the push stronger, because the cochlea is full of liquid and liquid is harder to move than air. In the cochlea the liquid ripples, and the tufts on the hair cells bend. Each bend makes a hair cell send a signal along the auditory nerve. Only then does the brain make the sound you hear.
examples: A pressure cooker whistle: vibrating steam, then air, eardrum, three bones, cochlea, hair cells, nerve, brain.
Your mother calling you from the kitchen reaches your brain through the same chain in much less than one second.
explanations.art: A cut-away ear in labelled steps: ear flap, ear canal, eardrum, three tiny bones, snail-shaped cochlea and the nerve going to the brain, with a bell ringing outside.
explanations.context: This card follows one sound through the ear, part by part.

explanations.concept: The quietest sound you can hear
explanations.definition: Every ear has a quietest sound it can catch, called the hearing threshold. A softer sound still reaches the ear, but it does not make a strong enough signal to be heard.
explanations.description: In the volume test, the phone was playing at the lowest steps, but you heard nothing. The sound was there in the air. It was too soft for your hair cells to send a clear signal. When the volume went up, you heard it. Covering the ear raised the step you needed, because less sound got in. An audiologist tests hearing this way. They play soft beeps of different pitches and find the quietest one you hear for each pitch.
examples: A ticking wall clock you can hear at night, but not in the day when the road is busy.
A child who hears a whisper from 3 metres away, while a grandparent needs the speaker to come closer.
explanations.art: A phone volume bar with grey steps at the bottom and a child's raised hand at the step where the song is first heard.
explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the volume test.

explanations.concept: Pitch, and the band of sounds people hear
explanations.definition: Pitch depends on how many times each second a thing vibrates. People hear from about 20 to about 20,000 vibrations each second, called 20 to 20,000 hertz.
explanations.description: A big drum skin vibrates slowly and makes a low pitch. A small bell vibrates very fast and makes a high pitch. Young people hear from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz. Sounds above that are called ultrasound. Sounds below it are called infrasound. They are real sounds, but our hair cells do not respond to them. Different hair cells pick up different pitches. Those for high sounds sit near the start of the coil in the cochlea, and those for low sounds sit deep inside it.
examples: A mosquito's whine is a few hundred hertz. You hear it well.
A dog whistle is above 20,000 hertz. A dog hears it, and you hear nothing.
explanations.art: A long band of colour from low to high pitch, with a person's ear covering the middle, an elephant at the low end and a bat at the high end.
explanations.context: This card explains pitch, and why some sounds are too high or too low for us.

explanations.concept: Why the highest sounds go first as we grow older
explanations.definition: The hair cells for the highest pitches wear out first, so most people hear less of the top of the band as they grow older.
explanations.description: High-pitch hair cells sit at the start of the cochlea, where every sound passes. Over many years, more of them stop working. A child may hear a tone of 17,000 hertz that most grown-ups over 40 cannot. Many grandparents hear deep voices well but miss high sounds, like the 's' and 'f' in words. So 'fifty' and 'sixty' can sound the same to them. Loud places and some illnesses make this happen sooner.
examples: A grandmother who hears the temple drum but misses the microwave beep.
In the family pitch test, the children hear the tone for longer than the parents.
explanations.art: Three family members in a row, a girl, her mother and her grandfather, each with a band of colour above them that is a little shorter at the high end than the one before.
explanations.context: This card explains why people of different ages hear different sounds.

explanations.definition: Very loud sound, or loud sound for a long time, can bend and break hair cells. In people, broken hair cells never grow back.
explanations.description: Loudness is measured in decibels. Talking is about 60 decibels. Sounds above about 85 decibels, heard for hours, slowly harm hearing. Very loud sounds close by, like a firecracker bursting near you, can harm it at once. After a loud wedding band or crackers, your ears may ring or sound muffled. That is a warning that hair cells were hurt. Most of it gets better in a day or so, but damage that happens again and again adds up. Birds can grow new hair cells, but people cannot.
examples: If you must shout to be heard by someone an arm's length away, the place is loud enough to harm hearing over time.
Earphones at full volume for hours each day can cause hearing loss that lasts.
explanations.art: A row of upright hair cell tufts, and next to it a row with some tufts bent flat after a loud noise.
explanations.context: This card explains why loud sound can harm hearing for ever.

explanations.definition: You protect your hearing by keeping loud sound short, keeping away from its source, covering your ears, and never pushing anything into the ear canal.
explanations.description: Moving away from a loud sound helps a lot, because sound spreads out and gets weaker with distance. Covering the ears helps, and a cover that seals the ear hole helps most. With earphones, keep the volume low enough to hear someone talking next to you. Earwax keeps the canal clean and moves out by itself as you chew and talk. A cotton bud can push wax deeper or scratch the eardrum. Doctors say to put nothing in your ear, not a bud, a hairpin, a matchstick or oil. If an ear hurts, leaks or feels blocked, see a doctor.
examples: Standing far back and pressing your ear flaps shut when crackers burst at Deepavali.
Wiping only the outside of the ear with a cloth after a bath.
explanations.art: A child at a Deepavali evening standing well back from bursting crackers, with fingertips pressing the small flaps over the ear holes.
explanations.context: This card is about protecting your hearing.

explanations.definition: Vibrations can reach the cochlea through the bones of the head, without passing through the eardrum. This is called bone conduction.
explanations.description: When you talk, your voice reaches your cochlea in two ways: through the air into your ears, and through the bones of your head. The bones carry the low parts of your voice well. That is why your voice sounds deeper to you than to others, and why a recording of your voice sounds strange. When you hum with your ears shut, the hum gets louder. Less sound escapes from the closed ear canal, and the hum still arrives through the bones.
examples: Your recorded voice sounds higher and thinner than the voice you hear when you talk.
Bhramari, the humming bee breath of yoga, is done with the ears shut, and the hum fills your head.
explanations.art: A child humming with thumbs closing the ear flaps, with wavy lines going through the jaw and skull straight to the cochlea.
explanations.context: This card explains the humming test, where your hum got louder with your ears shut.

explanations.concept: Animals that hear what we can't
explanations.definition: Many animals hear pitches that people cannot. Each one hears the sounds that matter for their way of living.
explanations.description: A moth flying at night has a problem: bats hunt moths in the dark. Many moths have ears on their bodies that hear the bats' ultrasound calls. When a bat comes close, the moth dives or zigzags away. Bats themselves call in ultrasound and listen to the echoes to find insects. A mouse is hunted by owls and cats, and mice call to each other in ultrasound. Cats and dogs hear higher sounds than we do. Elephants live in herds that spread out across a forest. Their low rumbles, partly infrasound, travel far, and other elephants hear them from kilometres away. A cricket hears with ears on her front legs.
examples: A dog hears a dog whistle that people cannot.
Pigeons hear infrasound, far below the lowest sound we can hear.
explanations.art: A night scene: a bat calling, a moth diving away, a cat with ears turned, and in the distance an elephant herd with long slow waves between them.
explanations.context: This card is about animals whose hearing goes beyond ours, and how it helps them live.

explanations.concept: What does a bat hear when the echoes come back?
explanations.description: A bat hears echoes of their own calls and knows where a moth is, how fast she flies and even her size. Nobody knows what this is like for the bat. Does it feel like seeing, or like hearing, or like something people have no word for? In 1974 the philosopher Thomas Nagel asked this question in an essay called 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?'. Scientists can measure what a bat's ears and brain do. They have no way yet to know what the bat experiences. Some blind people learn to click with their tongue and find walls and doorways from the echoes. They describe it in their own ways.
examples: A bat catches a moth in the dark in less than a second.
Some blind people find a doorway by clicking and listening to the echo.
explanations.art: A bat in the dark with a question mark made of curved sound lines beside them, and a moth ahead.
explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody can answer yet: what is hearing like for another creature?

agreed.text: The ear passes sound from the eardrum, through three tiny bones, to hair cells in the cochlea, which send signals to the brain.
agreed.evidence: Doctors and scientists have studied ears for centuries. Georg von Békésy watched the inside of the cochlea move with sound, and won the Nobel Prize in 1961.

agreed.text: In people, hair cells in the cochlea do not grow back once they are broken.
agreed.evidence: Doctors find damaged hair cells in the ears of people who worked for years in loud places. Birds can grow new hair cells. This was found in the late 1980s, and scientists are now trying to learn why people cannot.

agreed.text: Young people hear from about 20 to about 20,000 hertz, and the top of that band drops with age.
agreed.evidence: Audiologists test millions of people with beeps of different pitches. The same pattern shows up all over the world.

agreed.text: Many animals hear pitches people cannot: bats, moths, mice, cats and dogs hear ultrasound, and elephants and pigeons hear infrasound.
agreed.evidence: Scientists record these sounds with special microphones and test how animals react to them.

agreed.text: Loud sound for a long time causes hearing loss that lasts.
agreed.evidence: The World Health Organization studies hearing all over the world. It says that more than a billion young people are at risk from loud music and noisy places.

challenging.claim: Earwax is dirt, so ears must be cleaned out with cotton buds.
challenging.who: A very common idea in many homes
challenging.for: Earwax looks like dirt, and it is yellow or brown. Cotton buds are sold for ears.
challenging.against: Earwax is made by the ear on purpose. It traps dust and keeps the canal from drying out. It moves out on its own as you chew and talk. A cotton bud often pushes wax deeper and can scratch the canal or the eardrum.
challenging.context: This card is about a common habit: cleaning inside the ear.

challenging.claim: Putting oil in the ears is good for everyone.
challenging.who: A home remedy in many families
challenging.for: Oil can soften hard wax, and doctors sometimes advise ear drops to soften wax.
challenging.against: Doctors say to put nothing in the ear unless a doctor asks. If the eardrum has a tiny hole, or the ear has an infection, oil can make it worse. A healthy ear does not need oil.
challenging.context: This card is about a home remedy many families use.

challenging.claim: Only old people get hearing loss.
challenging.for: Hearing does get worse for most people as they grow old.
challenging.against: Loud music, earphones, firecrackers and noisy work can cause hearing loss in young people too. Some babies are born deaf or hearing less.
challenging.context: This card is about who can get hearing loss.

challenging.claim: If a sound does not hurt, it cannot harm your ears.
challenging.for: Very loud sound does hurt, and pain is a good warning.
challenging.against: Sound around 85 to 100 decibels does not hurt, but hours of it every day slowly break hair cells. Many people find out only years later.
challenging.context: This card is about whether pain is a good guide to safe sound.

challenging.claim: Animals with big ear flaps hear best.
challenging.for: Big ear flaps collect more sound. A rabbit or a fox turns them to catch faint sounds.
challenging.against: Bats, moths and crickets hear very well with tiny ears or none we can see. A moth's ears are on her body, and a cricket's are on her front legs. Hearing depends most on what is inside the ear.
challenging.context: This card is about whether big ears mean good hearing.

big_questions.q: When the phone played at the lowest volume and you heard nothing, was there a sound in the room or not?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the phone was doing, and what your ears were doing.

big_questions.q: A dog hears a whistle that you cannot. Which of you hears the room as it really is?
big_questions.hint: Could there be a creature that hears every sound? What would that be like?

big_questions.q: Your voice sounds different to you than to everyone else. Which one is your real voice?
big_questions.hint: Remember the recording, and the humming test with your ears shut.

big_questions.q: Hair cells in people do not grow back, but in birds they do. Why might that be?
big_questions.hint: Scientists don't know yet. Make your own guess and say why.

big_questions.q: If a forest is full of bat calls that no person can hear, is the forest noisy or quiet?
big_questions.hint: Who is the forest quiet for?

big_questions.q: What would your day be like if you heard everything a bat hears?
big_questions.hint: Think about the fan, the phone charger, the mice and the bats at night.

story.title: Appooppan and the Missing S
story.note: A made-up story set in Kochi. The hearing test is described as audiologists really do it.
text: Kavya was nine, and she lived in Kochi with her mother and her grandfather. She called him Appooppan, which means grandfather in Malayalam. For thirty years he had worked in a coir factory, where big machines twisted coconut fibre into rope all day.

Lately, Appooppan had started to get things wrong. Kavya told him her new teacher was called Miss Sumathi. He said, 'Miss Umathi? What a strange name.' She asked him for six bananas, and he brought her fifty paise. When the washing machine beeped, he didn't move. When her mother called from the kitchen, he heard every word.
'He hears Amma but not me,' Kavya said one evening. 'Is he ignoring me?'
'No,' said her mother. 'I think his ears are changing. We will go and see someone who knows.'

On Saturday they took the bus to a clinic in Ernakulam. The audiologist was a young woman called Dr Fathima. She sat Appooppan in a small quiet room with thick walls and gave him a pair of headphones.
'I will play some beeps,' she said. 'Some will be very soft. Each time you hear one, even a tiny one, raise your hand.'

Kavya watched through a window. Dr Fathima pressed keys on her laptop. A low beep came first. Appooppan's hand went up. She made it softer and softer, until his hand stayed down. Then she did the same with a higher beep, and a higher one.
On the screen, a line of dots appeared. For the low beeps, the dots sat near the top, close to a normal line. For the high beeps, the dots dropped down, far below it.

'This is called an audiogram,' Dr Fathima said, showing them. 'Each dot is the quietest beep he heard at that pitch. He hears low sounds well. High sounds have to be much louder before he hears them.'
'But the beeps were playing, even when his hand was down?' asked Kavya.
'Yes. The sound reached his ears. It was just too soft for him to catch.'

Dr Fathima drew a snail shell on a piece of paper. 'This is the cochlea, inside the ear. It is lined with tiny hair cells. The ones for high sounds sit here, at the start, where every sound passes. Over many years, many of them stop working. Thirty years of loud machines made it happen sooner.'
'Will they grow back?' Kavya asked.
'Not in people,' said Dr Fathima. 'A bird can grow new ones. We can't. That is why we protect our ears.'

Kavya thought about it on the bus home. The sound of 's' in 'Sumathi' and 'six' is a high hiss. Appooppan never heard the hiss, so 'six' sounded like nothing he knew. Her own voice was higher than Amma's. The washing machine beep was high too. Everything he missed was high.

That night she tried something. She sat in front of Appooppan, where he could see her face. She turned off the fan. She didn't shout, because shouting only made her voice higher and harder to understand. She spoke a little slower and a little lower. 'Appooppan, can I have SIX bananas?'
He laughed. 'Six! I heard it that time.'
A month later, Appooppan got two small hearing aids. They made high sounds louder, just for him. The first morning, he sat on the step and said, 'Kavya, what is that noise?'
She listened. It was a pair of sparrows on the wire. They had been chirping there every morning all year.
'Those are sparrows, Appooppan,' she said. 'They were always there. You just couldn't hear them.'
That evening, Kavya put a small packet of foam earplugs in the drawer by the door. 'For the temple festival,' she said. 'For the chenda drums. For both of us.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: the sound in the room was the same for Kavya and her grandfather. What differed was what each of their ears could catch. The hair cells for high pitches sit at the start of the cochlea and wear out first, and loud noise speeds this up. Facing the person, cutting background noise and speaking clearly and a little lower helps more than shouting.
ask: Why did Appooppan hear his daughter but often not Kavya?
When Appooppan's hand stayed down, was the beep still playing? How do you know?
Why did 'six' sound strange to him?
What did Kavya do to help him hear, and why did each thing help?
Why did Kavya buy earplugs for herself too?

games.title: Who Hears It? A card game of sounds and listeners
games.context: This is a card game about which creatures can hear which sounds. Some sounds are too high or too low for people, but other animals hear them.

printables.title: 8 listener cards (each shows which bands of pitch they hear)
items: A child: MIDDLE (all the sounds people hear)
A grandparent: MIDDLE, but often not its very top
An elephant: VERY LOW and the lower part of MIDDLE
A pigeon: VERY LOW and the lower part of MIDDLE
A cat: MIDDLE, HIGH and VERY HIGH
A mouse: MIDDLE, HIGH and VERY HIGH
A moth: HIGH, where bats call

printables.title: 10 sound cards (the band is on the back)
items: A veena string being plucked (back: MIDDLE)
A mosquito whining near your ear (back: MIDDLE)
A child saying 'six' (back: MIDDLE, with a high 's')
A tone of 17,000 hertz (back: top of the MIDDLE)
The lowest part of an elephant's rumble (back: VERY LOW)
The lowest rumble of a far-away storm (back: VERY LOW)
A bat hunting a moth (back: HIGH)
A baby mouse calling for their mother (back: VERY HIGH)

rules: Shuffle the listener cards. Each player takes two. Playing alone, take all eight.
Shuffle the sound cards and put them face down.
Turn over the top sound card and read it out. Don't look at the back yet.
Each player says which of their listeners can hear it, and why.
Turn the card over to check the band. Each right answer scores 1 point.
If a sound is heard by none of the people cards but by an animal, that player says how this hearing helps the animal's life, for 1 more point.
Play until all 10 sound cards are used. The highest score wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Explain the bands. VERY LOW is below 20 hertz. MIDDLE is 20 to 20,000 hertz, what people hear. HIGH is 20,000 to 60,000. VERY HIGH is above 60,000.
flow.say: People hear only the middle band. Some animals hear lower, and some hear higher.
flow.kid: Pick two listener cards. Look at their bands.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Who Hears It? game. Here you cut out the cards and learn the pitch bands.

flow.do: Play the rounds. After each card, ask why.
flow.say: A bat hunting a moth. Who at the table can hear it? Why does the moth need to?
flow.kid: Read the sound card. Can your listeners hear it? Say why.

ask.q: Why does a moth need to hear bats?
good: So she can dive away before the bat catches her.
Because bats hunt moths at night.

ask.q: Why does an elephant hear very low sounds?
good: Other elephants call with low rumbles from far away.
So the herd can stay together.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask the last question.
flow.say: Which listener heard the most cards? Did any listener hear them all?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Did anyone hear every sound?

check.q: Which creature in the game could hear a baby mouse calling for their mother?
check.why: Baby mice call in very high ultrasound. Cats hear very high sounds, which helps them find mice. People and elephants cannot hear such high sounds.

games.title: The Ear Road: a board game from ear flap to brain

flow.do: Set up the board and cards.

flow.kid: Put your counter on the ear flap. You are a sound!

flow.say: You landed on the eardrum. What does it do?
flow.kid: Say the part you landed on. What does it do?

flow.do: End the game and ask one question.
flow.say: Which card sent people back the most? Why is that habit harmful?
flow.kid: Which card sent you back? Why is it bad for ears?

check.q: Why does a cotton bud send you back 3 squares?

It makes the ear canal grow longer
check.why: Earwax moves out on its own. A bud pushes some of it back in, and can scratch the canal or the eardrum. Doctors say to put nothing in the ear.

experiments.title: The Quietest Sound: which ear cover blocks the most?
experiments.context: In this experiment you find the quietest sound you can hear from across a room. Then you test which ear cover makes you need the loudest sound, because that cover blocks the most.
experiments.question: Which ear cover blocks the most sound: cupped hands, a thick folded towel, or the small ear flaps pressed shut with a fingertip?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which cover will block the most sound: cupped hands, a folded towel, or pressing the small flaps shut? Which will block the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the ear cover: the same phone, the same song, the same distance of 3 metres, the same quiet room. The helper turns the volume up one step at a time, slowly and evenly. The listener keeps their eyes shut so they can't see the phone. Try each cover twice, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: How many steps more than open ears?

materials.item: a phone that can play a song, with volume buttons
a quiet room with the fan and TV off, and a space about 3 metres long
a chair for the listener
a thick hand towel or a small folded bedsheet
a measuring tape, or count 4 big steps of a grown-up for about 3 metres
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Nothing goes inside the ear. Press only the small flap in front of the ear hole. Keep the phone at least 3 metres away, and stop when the listener hears the song. The volume never needs to be loud.

schedule.what: Find the quietest volume step you can hear with open ears. Repeat with cupped hands, a towel and the ear flaps pressed shut. Compare the steps.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw one bar for each ear cover, as tall as the volume step it needed.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan, the TV and anything humming. 2. Put the chair at one end of the room. 3. Measure 3 metres and put the phone there, speaker facing the chair. 4. Start a song and turn the volume all the way down.
flow.say: The song is playing, but the volume is at zero. We will turn it up one step at a time. You tell me the moment you hear it.
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. The phone is 3 metres away. A song is playing very, very softly. Can you hear it yet?
flow.parent: Pick a song with steady sound, not a quiet start. Check that the phone does not lock or pause. On most phones, pressing the volume button once moves one step. Counting steps is easier if the phone shows a volume bar.
flow.context: This is the first step of the quietest sound test. Here you set up a quiet room with a phone 3 metres away.

flow.do: Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Soon you will cover your ears in three ways. Which do you think will block the most sound? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which cover blocks most: hands, a towel, or pressing the flaps shut? Why?

ask.q: Which cover do you think will block the most, and why?
good: The towel, because it is thick and soft.
Pressing the flaps, because it closes the hole.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.do: 1. The listener shuts their eyes. 2. Press the volume up one step every 3 seconds. Count the steps out loud in your head. 3. When the listener raises a hand, write down the step. 4. Turn it back to zero. Do it once more.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Raise your hand the moment you hear the song, even a tiny bit.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Listen hard. Raise your hand when you hear the song.
flow.parent: Once in a while, wait without pressing anything for a few seconds. If a hand goes up then, the listener is guessing. Ask them to raise it only when they are sure. This is what audiologists do too. If the listener hears step 1 straight away, move the chair further back, or put the phone in the next room with the door open.
flow.context: In this step you find the quietest volume step the listener can hear with open ears.

flow.do: 1. Now test each ear cover the same way, twice each. 2. Cupped hands: palms held over both ear flaps. 3. Towel: folded thick and held over both ears with both hands. 4. Ear flaps: press the small flap in front of each ear hole shut with a fingertip. 5. Write each step in the table.
flow.say: Same phone, same place, same song. Only the ear cover changes. Raise your hand when you hear it.
flow.kid: Cover your ears the new way. Shut your eyes. Raise your hand when you hear it.
flow.parent: Show the small flap: it is the bump of cartilage just in front of the ear hole. Pushing it back over the hole closes the hole without putting anything inside. If the listener cannot hear the song even at full volume with a cover, write 'more than full' and move closer for every test.
flow.context: In this step you test three ear covers in the same way.

flow.do: 1. For each cover, take away the open-ears step from its step. 2. Write the difference in the last column.
flow.say: Which cover needed the most extra steps? That one blocked the most sound. Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Which cover needed the most steps? That one blocked most. Were you right?

check.q: Arjun heard the song at step 2 with open ears and at step 7 with his ear flaps pressed shut. What does that tell you?
options: Pressing the flaps made the song quieter at the phone
Pressing the flaps blocked sound, so he needed a louder song to hear it
check.why: The phone played the same at each step. What changed was how much sound got into Arjun's ears. With the flaps shut, less got in, so the song had to be louder before he caught it. His hearing is fine: open the flaps and he hears step 2 again.

flow.do: Talk about the results. Then go back to step 1 of the volume, with the song still playing and ears open.
flow.say: Look. At step 1 the song is playing, but you can't hear it. What is happening to that sound?
flow.kid: The song plays at step 1. You can't hear it. Where is the sound going?

ask.q: Why did one cover block more than another?
good: It closed the ear hole, so sound couldn't get in round the edges.
Hands leave gaps, and sound goes through gaps.

ask.q: At step 1, is there sound in the room?
good: Yes, the phone is making sound, but it is too soft for my ears.
Yes, a cat might hear it.

flow.think: Is a room ever truly silent?
flow.parent: Usually the pressed flaps need the most extra steps, because they seal the ear hole. Cupped hands leave gaps, and sound slips round them. A towel blocks more when pressed tight. Your family's results may differ, and that is fine. Ask what they found, not what the book says.

experiments.title: Who Hears the Highest Note? A family pitch test
experiments.context: In this experiment the whole family listens to a tone that rises higher and higher. Each person raises a hand when they stop hearing it. You find out who hears the highest pitch.
experiments.question: Who in our family can hear the highest pitch: the children or the grown-ups?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Who in your family will hear the highest note? Who will stop hearing it first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone sits at the same distance from the same phone, with the same volume. The tone goes up in the same steps for everyone. Each person listens with eyes shut, so they don't copy anyone. Test each person twice.

materials.item: a phone or computer that can open a free online tone generator (see the links)
family members of different ages: at least one child and one grown-up
paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up sets the volume first, at 1,000 hertz, to a comfortable talking level. Never turn it up for the high notes. Don't use earphones for this test. Stop if anyone finds the sound unpleasant.

schedule.what: Play a tone that rises from 8,000 hertz. Each person raises a hand when they stop hearing it. Write down the number.

experiments.record: Write each person's name, age and the highest pitch they heard. Put them in order from the highest to the lowest.

flow.do: 1. Open the tone generator. 2. Set it to 1,000 hertz. 3. Set the volume to a comfortable talking level. 4. Put the phone on a table 1 metre from where everyone sits.
flow.say: This plays one pure note. The number is how many times each second the speaker vibrates. Let's hear 1,000 first.
flow.kid: Listen to the note. Its speaker vibrates 1,000 times a second. Is it high or low?
flow.parent: Use the device's own speaker, not earphones. Leave the volume at this level for the whole test. Higher notes can sound sharp, so keep it moderate.
flow.context: This is the first step of the family pitch test. Here a grown-up sets up a tone generator at a safe volume.

flow.do: Ask everyone for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will make the note higher and higher. Who do you think will hear it the longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Who will hear the highest note? You, or the grown-ups? Why?

ask.q: Who do you think will hear the highest note, and why?
good: Me, because children hear better.
Amma, because she is bigger.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.do: 1. Start at 8,000 hertz. 2. Raise it by 1,000 hertz every 5 seconds. 3. Everyone listens with eyes shut and raises a hand when the note disappears. 4. Write down the number for each person. 5. Do it twice.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Raise your hand when you can't hear the note any more.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. The note goes higher. Raise your hand when it disappears.
flow.parent: Phone speakers often can't play very high notes well. If everyone stops at the same number, the speaker may be the limit, not the ears. Then try a laptop or a speaker. Many grown-ups over 40 stop somewhere between 12,000 and 16,000 hertz. Many children still hear 17,000 or more.
flow.context: In this step everyone listens as the note rises, and each person shows when they stop hearing it.

flow.do: Put everyone in order from the highest pitch heard to the lowest. Look for a pattern with age.
flow.say: Who heard the highest? Who stopped first? Do you see a pattern with age?
flow.kid: Who heard the highest note? Is there a pattern with age?

check.q: Meenakshi, aged 8, hears the note up to 18,000 hertz. Her grandmother stops at 9,000. Why?
options: Hair cells for the highest pitches wear out first as people grow older
Older people hear only low sounds
check.why: The hair cells for the highest pitches sit at the start of the cochlea, and they wear out first over the years. The grandmother still hears many high sounds, just not the very highest. 'Only low sounds' goes too far.

flow.do: Play 20,000 hertz for a few seconds, then switch it off.
flow.say: Most of us hear nothing now, but the speaker is still vibrating. A dog or a cat would hear this easily.
flow.kid: The speaker is still vibrating. Can you hear it? A dog could!

ask.q: Is there a sound in the room right now?
good: Yes, the speaker is vibrating, but it is too high for us.
For a dog, yes.

flow.think: What else in our home might make sounds too high for us?

experiments.title: Through the Door: do low or high sounds pass better?
experiments.context: In this experiment you play a low note and a high note behind a closed door. You find out which one the door blocks more.
experiments.question: When a door is shut, does a low note or a high note get through better?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Behind a shut door, will the low note or the high note sound quieter? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same phone, the same volume and the same place for both notes. Listen from the same spot, first with the door open, then shut. Only the pitch and the door change.
results_table: Door open: how loud (3 big, 2 medium, 1 soft, 0 nothing)

materials.item: a phone with a free online tone generator
a room with a door that shuts
a helper

experiments.safety: Keep the volume at a comfortable talking level. Don't hold the phone near anyone's ear.

schedule.what: Play a 200 hertz note and a 4,000 hertz note behind a door, open and shut. Score how loud each sounds.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle the note that lost more loudness when the door shut.

flow.do: 1. Put the phone on a table inside the room. 2. Set the volume to a comfortable level. 3. Stand outside, 2 metres from the open door.
flow.say: We will play a low note and a high note. First, guess: which will the door block more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the door block the low note or the high note more? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the door test. Here you set up a phone inside a room and stand outside.

flow.do: 1. The helper plays 200 hertz. 2. Score how loud it sounds with the door open. 3. Shut the door and score it again. 4. Do the same with 4,000 hertz.
flow.say: Score it: 3 for big, 2 for medium, 1 for soft, 0 for nothing.
flow.kid: Listen. Give it a score from 0 to 3. Now the door shuts. Score it again.
flow.parent: The helper must not change the volume between notes. Low notes often sound softer than high notes at the same volume, because ears are less sensitive to them. That is why we compare how much each note drops when the door shuts.

flow.do: Work out how much each note dropped.
flow.say: Which note dropped more when the door shut?
flow.kid: Which note lost more when the door shut?

check.q: Lakshmi hears her neighbour's music through the wall. She hears the drum beat but not the words. Why?
options: Walls and doors block high sounds more than low sounds
check.why: Walls and doors block high pitches more than low pitches. Words need high sounds like 's' and 't' to be understood, so they get lost. The low drum gets through. Elephants use this: low rumbles travel far and pass through forests.

flow.do: Talk about elephants.
flow.say: Elephants call with very low rumbles. Why might low sounds be useful for a herd spread across a forest?
flow.kid: Elephants rumble very low. Why is low good in a big forest?

ask.q: Why might low rumbles help an elephant herd?
good: Low sounds pass through trees and travel far.
The herd can stay in touch from far away.

flow.parent: In your test the high note usually drops more. If both dropped the same, the door may have a big gap. Try a heavier door.

activities.title: Hum With Your Ears Shut
activities.context: This is a quick way to start the unit. You hum with your ears open, then with them shut, and notice something surprising.

materials.item: your own voice and hands

activities.safety: Press only the small flaps over the ear holes. Never push a finger inside the ear.

schedule.what: Hum with ears open, then with the ear flaps pressed shut. Compare.

activities.record: Write one sentence: what happened to your hum when your ears were shut?

flow.do: 1. Sit up straight. 2. Hum one long 'mmm' with your ears open.
flow.say: Let's hum together, one long note. Listen to how loud it sounds to you.
flow.kid: Hum one long 'mmm'. Listen to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the humming test. Here you hum with your ears open.

flow.do: 1. Press the small flap in front of each ear hole shut with your thumbs. 2. Before humming, ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Hum the same note again.
flow.say: Now we close our ears. Will the hum sound louder, quieter or the same? Why do you think so? Now hum.
flow.kid: Press your ear flaps shut. Guess: louder or quieter? Why? Now hum.

good: It got louder!
It filled my head.

flow.parent: Most people are surprised that the hum gets louder. In yoga this is Bhramari, the humming bee breath, done with the ears closed.

flow.do: Ask how the sound could get in with the ears shut.
flow.say: Your ears were shut, but the hum got louder. How did it reach you?
flow.kid: Your ears were shut. How did the hum get in?

check.q: With your ears shut, your hum sounds louder. How does it reach your cochlea?
options: Through the bones of your head
Through tiny gaps around your thumbs
It doesn't, you only imagine it
check.why: Your voice vibrates the bones of your head, and they carry the vibration straight to the cochlea. With the ear hole shut, less of the hum escapes, so it sounds louder. This is called bone conduction.

activities.title: Is That Really My Voice?
activities.context: In this activity you record your own voice and play it back. Most people are surprised by how they sound.

materials.item: a phone that can record sound

schedule.what: Record a sentence, play it back, and compare it with how you hear yourself.

activities.record: Write one word for how your voice sounds to you, and one for how it sounds on the recording.

flow.do: 1. Open the voice recorder. 2. Each person says one sentence, like 'My name is Kavya and I like dosa.'
flow.say: Say your sentence. Then we will play it back.
flow.kid: Say your name and your favourite food. The phone records it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the voice recording activity. Here everyone records one sentence.

flow.do: 1. Play each recording. 2. Ask each person if they sound like themselves.
flow.say: Do you sound like you? Now ask Amma: is that how you always sound to her?
flow.kid: Listen. Is that your voice? Ask Amma if it sounds like you.

ask.q: What is different about your recorded voice?
good: It sounds higher.
It sounds thinner.
It doesn't sound like me.

flow.do: Explain why, after the child has said what they noticed.
flow.say: When you talk, you hear yourself through the air and through the bones of your head. The bones carry the low parts best. Everyone else hears only the air part.
flow.kid: You hear yourself through your bones too. Others hear only the air part.
flow.think: Which one is your real voice?

setup.caption: 1. Record one sentence.

setup.art: The girl listening to the phone with a surprised face, and her mother smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Play it back. Does it sound like you?

activities.title: Turn Your Ears Like a Cat
activities.context: In this activity you use your hands to make your ear flaps bigger and turn them, as a cat does. You hear what difference it makes.

materials.item: a fan, a ticking clock or a phone playing soft music

schedule.what: Cup hands behind your ears, then in front facing backwards, and compare.

activities.record: Draw your hands for the way that made the sound in front loudest, and the way that made a sound behind you loudest.

flow.do: 1. Stand facing the fan or phone, 2 metres away. 2. Listen. 3. Cup both hands behind your ear flaps, fingers together, and listen again.
flow.say: Listen to the fan. Now cup your hands behind your ears. Is it louder, quieter or the same?
flow.kid: Listen. Now cup your hands behind your ears. Louder or quieter?
flow.context: This is the first step of the cat ears activity. Here you make your ear flaps bigger with your hands.

flow.do: 1. Turn your back to the sound. 2. Hold your cupped hands in front of your ears, open side facing backwards. 3. Listen.
flow.say: Now the sound is behind you. Turn your hand cups to face it. What happens?
flow.kid: Turn around. Face your hand cups backwards. Is the sound louder now?

ask.q: Why does turning the cups help?
good: They catch the sound coming from that side.
Like a cat turning their ears.

flow.do: Talk about cats.
flow.say: A cat can turn each ear flap separately, without moving the head. Why would that help a cat who hunts mice?
flow.kid: A cat turns each ear on their own. Why does that help catch a mouse?

ask.q: How does turning ears help a cat?
good: They can hear a mouse rustling and find which way it is.
They can listen in two directions at once.

activities.title: Build a Model Ear
activities.context: In this activity you build a model of the ear from paper, a balloon and a few small things. It shows the chain a sound passes along.

materials.item: a sheet of chart paper or a newspaper page
a toilet roll tube or a rolled paper tube
a piece of balloon or thin plastic and a rubber band
three small things, like grains of rajma, beads or bits of pasta
a length of wool or a strip of clay, for the cochlea
glue or tape, and a felt pen

schedule.what: Build and label a model ear from the ear flap to the cochlea.

activities.record: Label each part and write one line about what it does.

flow.do: 1. Cut an ear flap shape from the chart paper. 2. Tape it to one end of the tube.
flow.say: The ear flap collects sound. The tube is the ear canal.
flow.kid: Cut out an ear flap. Stick it on the tube. That is the ear canal.
flow.context: This is the first step of the model ear. Here you make the ear flap and the ear canal.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the balloon piece over the other end of the tube. 2. Hold it with a rubber band.
flow.say: This is the eardrum. Tap the tube and feel it vibrate.
flow.kid: Stretch the balloon over the end. That is your eardrum.
flow.parent: If you sprinkle a few grains of salt on the eardrum and shout into the flap, they may jump. It is a bonus, not a must.

flow.do: 1. Glue the three small things in a row behind the eardrum on a sheet. 2. Coil the wool like a snail shell next to them.
flow.say: These are the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. The coil is the cochlea.
flow.kid: Glue three tiny things in a row. Coil the wool like a snail.

ask.q: What do the three tiny bones do?
good: They pass the vibration from the eardrum to the cochlea.
They make the push stronger.

flow.do: Label every part. Draw a line from the cochlea to a small brain.
flow.say: Tell me the journey of a sound, from the flap to the brain.
flow.kid: Label each part. Tell the journey of a sound out loud.

check.q: Which part turns the vibration into signals for the brain?
options: The hair cells in the cochlea
check.why: The eardrum and bones pass the vibration on. Only the hair cells in the cochlea turn it into nerve signals. Picking the eardrum is a common mix-up, because it is the part that shakes first.

activities.title: The Arm's-Length Noise Check
activities.context: In this activity you check which sounds at home are loud enough to harm hearing over time, using one simple test.

materials.item: a helper
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Don't stand close to a pressure cooker as it whistles. Stay at a safe distance from anything hot.

schedule.what: Do the arm's-length test next to the mixer, the TV, the balcony and anywhere else noisy.

activities.record: Make two lists: 'normal voice is fine' and 'had to shout'.

flow.do: Explain the test.
flow.say: Here is a test doctors use. Stand one arm's length from someone. If you have to shout to be heard, the place is loud enough to harm ears over time.
flow.kid: Stand an arm's length from Amma. Talk. Do you need to shout?
flow.context: This is the first step of the noise check. Here you learn a simple test for harmful noise.

flow.do: 1. Try the test in a quiet room. 2. Next to the mixer grinder while it runs. 3. Near the TV at its usual volume. 4. On the balcony or at the window when traffic is busy.
flow.say: Say 'Can you hear me?' in a normal voice. Did I hear you, or did you have to shout?
flow.kid: Say 'Can you hear me?' in a normal voice. Did you need to shout?
flow.parent: A mixer grinder is often loud enough to fail the test. It is fine for a minute, but shutting the kitchen door or stepping out helps.

flow.do: Make the two lists and pick one change.
flow.say: Which loud thing could we make shorter, or move away from?
flow.kid: Pick one loud thing. How can we keep our ears safe from it?

good: Shut the kitchen door when the mixer runs.
Turn the TV down.
Close the window in busy traffic.

activities.title: Why Do Ears Pop? The tube to your throat
activities.context: In this activity you feel the tiny tube that joins each ear to the back of your throat. It is why ears pop in a lift or on a ghat road.

materials.item: a glass of water

activities.safety: Don't blow hard with your nose pinched. Swallowing gently is enough.

schedule.what: Swallow with your nose pinched and listen for a small click in your ears.

activities.record: Write one sentence about when your ears have popped before.

flow.do: 1. Pinch your nose gently. 2. Take a sip of water and swallow.
flow.say: Swallow with your nose pinched. Did you hear or feel a little click in your ears?
flow.kid: Pinch your nose. Swallow some water. Feel a click?
flow.context: This is the first step of the ear popping activity. Here you feel the tube behind your eardrum open.

flow.do: Explain, after asking for ideas.
flow.say: Behind each eardrum is a little space full of air. A thin tube joins it to your throat. When you swallow, the tube opens, and the air on both sides of the eardrum evens out.
flow.kid: A tiny tube joins your ear to your throat. Swallowing opens it.

good: In a lift.
Driving up the ghat road to Ooty.
In an aeroplane.

flow.parent: This is the Eustachian tube. Going up a hill, the air outside gets thinner, the eardrum bulges, and sounds seem muffled until a swallow or a yawn opens the tube.

projects.title: Our Family Noise Diary
projects.context: In this 5-day project the family notes every loud moment of the day. Then you make a plan to protect everyone's ears.

materials.item: a notebook or a sheet of paper with a table
a clock or a phone to check times

projects.safety: Use the arm's-length test only. Don't go close to firecrackers, loudspeakers or horns to test them.

schedule.what: Draw the diary table. Note every loud moment today and how many minutes it lasted.
Keep the diary. Use the arm's-length test for each loud moment.
Keep the diary. Notice loud sounds outside the home too.
Keep the diary. Add up the loud minutes for each day.
Look at the totals. Make a family plan with three changes, and draw a poster.

projects.record: A table with the time, the loud sound, how long it lasted and whether you had to shout. A total for each day.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with four columns: time, loud sound, minutes, had to shout? 2. Fill it in through the day.
flow.say: For five days we will be noise detectives. Every time something is loud, we write it down.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Write each loud sound you hear today.
flow.context: This is the first step of the noise diary. Here you set up the table and start noting loud moments.

flow.do: Keep the diary on days 2, 3 and 4. On day 4, add up the minutes for each day.
flow.say: Remember the arm's-length test. Did we have to shout?
flow.kid: Keep writing loud moments. Add up the minutes.
flow.wait: Keep the diary for 3 more days
flow.parent: Common entries: the mixer grinder, the pressure cooker, honking traffic, a loud TV, a festival loudspeaker.

flow.do: 1. Look at the totals. 2. Pick the three loudest or longest. 3. Make a plan for each and draw a poster.
flow.say: Which loud sounds take the most minutes? What could we change?
flow.kid: Which sound is loudest? Which lasts longest? Make a plan.

ask.q: What is one change our family can make?
good: Close the kitchen door when the mixer runs.
Keep earphone volume low.
Stand far back at the crackers.

challenges.title: Earmuffs for the Festival
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make the best ear protectors you can from home things, and test them with the volume test.
challenges.problem: At the temple festival, the chenda drums and firecrackers are very loud. Your little cousin is 4 and hates it. Design ear protectors from home things that block the most sound and are comfortable.
constraints: Nothing may go inside the ear canal.
It must stay on while walking.
materials: a headband or a strip of cloth
cotton wool, a sponge or folded cloth
the phone from the volume test
general: Shop-bought earmuffs: hard cups with soft foam rims that seal around the ear flap.
Foam earplugs, for older children and grown-ups, rolled small and placed at the ear hole as the packet shows.
Standing further away, which works for everyone.
creative: Two plastic cups lined with a folded cloth, joined by a headband.
A thick woollen cap pulled down over the ears.
A dupatta wrapped round the head, with folded cloth over each ear.
challenges.your_turn: Design and build your own ear protectors. Test them with the volume test from the quietest sound experiment. How many steps more than open ears did they need?

flow.do: Read the problem. Remember the volume test.
flow.say: In the volume test, which cover blocked the most? What made it good?
flow.kid: Which cover worked best in the volume test? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the festival earmuff challenge. Here you think about what made a good ear cover.

flow.do: Draw two designs.
flow.say: Draw two ideas. Which one seals the ear best? Which one is comfy?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. Which seals best?

flow.do: Build the best design.
flow.say: Build it. Remember: nothing goes inside the ear.
flow.kid: Build your earmuffs. Nothing goes inside the ear!
flow.parent: Help with cutting. Check nothing is tight on the head.

flow.do: Test it with the volume test, twice.
flow.say: Let's test. At which step do you hear the song now?
flow.kid: Put them on. Shut your eyes. Raise your hand when you hear it.

check.q: Riya's cup earmuffs block 2 steps. Her sister's cloth-lined cups block 4 steps. Why might the lining help?
options: It fills the gaps, so less sound leaks round the edges
check.why: Sound slips through any gap. A soft lining presses against the head and closes the gaps, so less sound gets in. Real earmuffs have soft foam rims for the same reason.

setup.caption: 1. Gather home things.

setup.art: A child wearing two plastic cups lined with cloth, joined by a headband, raising a hand in the volume test.
setup.caption: 2. Build your earmuffs and test them.

challenges.title: Talk So Appooppan Can Hear
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You find the best ways to talk to someone who hears high sounds less well.
challenges.problem: Many grandparents hear low sounds but miss high ones, like the 's' in 'six'. Shouting often makes it worse. Find the ways of talking that work best.
constraints: You must test each idea, not just guess.
The listener must not see a written word.
materials: a list of 10 words that sound alike, such as six, fix, fish, fifty, sixty
general: Face the person, so they can see your lips.
Turn off the fan, the TV and the mixer.
Speak a little slower and a little lower, not louder.
creative: A clap before you speak, so the person turns to you.
A light or a wave to call them from another room.
A small notebook for important words, like a time or a number.
challenges.your_turn: Choose the three ways that worked best in your test. Teach them to your family.

flow.do: The listener presses their ear flaps shut, to hear less, like someone with hearing loss.
flow.say: With your flaps shut, you will hear less. Now let's find which way of talking helps most.
flow.kid: Press your ear flaps shut. Now you hear less.
flow.context: This is the first step of the talking challenge. Here the listener blocks their ears a little.

flow.do: 1. Say five words from behind the listener, in a normal voice. 2. Then face them. 3. Then turn off the fan and speak slowly. 4. Then shout. 5. Count how many words they get right each time.
flow.say: Tell me each word you hear. I will count the right ones.
flow.kid: Say each word you hear. Your partner counts the right ones.
flow.parent: Shouting makes the voice higher and blurs the sounds, so it often scores worst. Facing the person usually helps most.

flow.do: Compare the counts. Pick the best three ways.
flow.say: Which way got the most words right? Did shouting help?
flow.kid: Which way worked best? Did shouting help?

check.q: Why does facing someone help them understand you?
options: They can see your lips and face
check.why: Everyone reads lips a little, and people who hear less read them more. Your face also shows which words you are saying. Sound does go in all directions, but more of it goes the way you face.
