quiz.p: Which part of the ear vibrates first when a sound arrives?
quiz.why: The ear flap and canal collect and lead the sound in, and the eardrum is the first part that vibrates. Then the bones, then the cochlea.

quiz.p: Where are the hair cells that turn vibrations into signals?
quiz.why: Hair cells line the cochlea, the snail-shaped tube deep inside the head. Picking 'ear canal' mixes up hair cells with the tiny hairs near the ear hole.

quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3, turns a phone up one step at a time from across the room. Her brother first hears the song at step 3. What is step 3?
opts: The loudest sound he can hear
The quietest sound he can hear from there
quiz.why: Below step 3 the phone was playing, but too softly for him to catch. Step 3 is his quietest sound at that distance.

quiz.p: In a fair test of ear covers, what must change?
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the phone or distance changed too, you couldn't tell what caused the difference.

quiz.p: Why can loud sound cause hearing loss that never gets better?
opts: It makes the ear canal smaller
It breaks hair cells, and in people they do not grow back
It makes the ear flap stiff
quiz.why: Hair cells bend and break under loud sound. Birds can grow new ones, but people cannot, so the loss stays.

quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 4, has to shout to be heard by her friend, an arm's length away. What does that tell her?
opts: The place is loud enough to harm hearing over time
quiz.why: This is the arm's-length test. If you must shout at an arm's length, the sound is loud enough to harm hearing if you stay long.

quiz.p: What is the safest way to look after earwax?
opts: Clean it out with a cotton bud every day
Leave it, and wipe only the outside of the ear
quiz.why: Earwax traps dust and moves out by itself. Pushing anything in can push wax deeper or harm the eardrum.

quiz.p: Why do many moths have ears that hear bat calls?
opts: To hear a hunting bat and dive away
quiz.why: Bats hunt moths at night with ultrasound calls. A moth who hears the calls can dive or zigzag and escape.

quiz.p: Which animal hears sounds too low for people?
quiz.why: Elephants hear infrasound, which is too low for us. Their low rumbles help herd members keep in touch over long distances.

quiz.p: A drum skin vibrates slowly. A small bell vibrates very fast. Which has the higher pitch?
quiz.why: Faster vibration makes a higher pitch. Pitch is counted in hertz, vibrations each second.

quiz.p: Most children can hear a tone of 17,000 hertz that many grandparents cannot. Why?
opts: Grandparents' hair cells for the highest pitches have worn out
Grandparents don't want to hear it
quiz.why: Hair cells for the highest pitches wear out first as people grow older, so the top of the band drops.

quiz.p: A dog barks at a whistle that you can't hear at all. What is happening?
opts: The whistle makes ultrasound, which dogs hear and people don't
quiz.why: Dog whistles vibrate above 20,000 hertz. That is ultrasound: above our band, but inside a dog's.

items.p: A bell rings. Put the parts of the ear in the order the sound reaches them.
items.why: The ear flap collects the sound, the ear canal leads it in, and the eardrum vibrates. The three tiny bones pass the vibration to the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into signals. The auditory nerve carries them to the brain.

items.p: Match each part of the ear to what it does.
pairs: pass the vibration to the cochlea
carries the signals to the brain
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part does one job in a chain. A strong answer could also say what goes wrong if one part is missing.

items.p: In the volume test, Kavya hears the song at step 2 with open ears. With cupped hands she hears it at step 3. What does the cupped-hands result tell you?
opts: Her hands blocked a little sound
Her hands made the phone quieter
items.why: The phone played the same at each step. Her hands let less sound into her ears, so the song had to be one step louder. Hands leave gaps, so they block only a little.

items.p: In the volume test, the phone was playing at step 1, but you heard nothing. Was there a sound in the room? Explain.
items.a: Yes. The phone was vibrating and sending out sound, but it was softer than the quietest sound my ears can catch. So I didn't hear it.
items.why: A strong answer separates the sound in the air from the hearing in the ear.

items.p: Farhan says, 'Earwax is dirt. I should clean it out every day with a cotton bud.' Is he right?
items.why: False. Earwax is made by the ear on purpose. It traps dust and moves out by itself. A cotton bud can push it deeper or scratch the eardrum. A strong answer says what earwax does and what to do instead: wipe only the outside.

items.p: How high or low a sound is, is called its ____.
items.why: Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates. Faster vibration makes a higher pitch.

items.p: Which of these can harm hearing for ever?
opts: Listening to earphones at full volume for hours every day
items.why: Loud sound for a long time breaks hair cells in the cochlea, and in people they never grow back. Earphones put the loud sound right at the ear.

items.p: Draw the ear from the side, cut open, and label the ear flap, ear canal, eardrum, three tiny bones and cochlea.
items.a: A drawing with the ear flap outside, a tube going in, a thin skin at its end, three small bones behind it and a snail-shaped coil.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the parts in the right order and shows the cochlea as a coil.
items.art: A blank outline of a head from the side.

items.p: Sort these habits: good for ears, or harmful for ears?
items: pushing a hairpin into the ear
sitting next to a loudspeaker at a wedding
wiping only the outside of the ear
putting a cotton bud deep in the ear
items.a: see items
items.why: Distance, low volume and leaving the canal alone protect hearing. Pushing things in and staying close to loud sounds harm it.

items.p: A moth hears a bat's call coming closer. What does the moth do?
opts: Stops and lands on the bat
Nothing, because moths have no ears
items.why: Many moths have ears on their bodies that hear bat calls. Diving away helps them escape being eaten.

items.p: Your hum got louder when you pressed your ear flaps shut. How did the sound reach your cochlea?
items.a: Through the bones of my head. My voice made my bones vibrate, and they carried the vibration to the cochlea. With the ear shut, less of the hum escaped.
items.why: A strong answer names bone conduction, or says the bones carried the vibration.

items.p: Label the three tiny bones in the picture: hammer, anvil, stirrup.
items.why: The hammer touches the eardrum, the anvil is in the middle, and the stirrup pushes on the cochlea. The stirrup is the smallest bone in the body.
items.art: Three tiny linked bones between an eardrum and a coil, with three blank label lines.

items.p: People can hear every sound there is.
items.why: False. People hear only from about 20 to about 20,000 hertz. Sounds above and below that are real, and many animals hear them.

items.p: Why do your ears pop when you drive up a ghat road to Munnar?
opts: The air outside gets thinner, and the tube to your throat opens to even out the air
items.why: Higher up, the air pressure is lower. The air behind the eardrum pushes outwards until a swallow opens the tube to the throat and evens it out. That is the pop.

items.p: Two friends in Madurai are at a wedding with a very loud band.

views.says: It doesn't hurt, so it can't harm my ears. I'll stay right at the front.
We had to shout to talk. I'm going to stand at the back.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use the arm's-length test and what you know about hair cells. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Nandini, because having to shout at arm's length means the sound is loud enough to harm hearing over time, and hair cells don't grow back. It gives Divya her due: pain is a real warning sign, and a short time near loud music is not a disaster. But no pain doesn't mean no harm.
items.why: Both have part of it. Pain is a warning, but harm can start below the level that hurts.

items.p: Sound that is too high for people to hear is called ____.
items.why: Ultra means beyond. Ultrasound is above about 20,000 hertz. Bats, dogs, cats and mice hear it.

items.p: Nithya's results in the volume test: open ears step 2, cupped hands step 3, towel step 5, ear flaps pressed shut step 8. Which cover blocked the most?
items.why: The flaps needed 8 steps, 6 more than open ears, so they blocked the most. They seal the ear hole, while hands and towels leave gaps.

items.p: Why do you think pressing the ear flaps shut blocked more sound than cupping your hands?
items.a: Pressing the flap closes the ear hole completely. Cupped hands leave gaps between the fingers and round the edges, and sound slips through gaps.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of gaps or sealing.

items.p: In the family pitch test, Arjun, aged 7, hears up to 18,000 hertz and his father, aged 45, up to 14,000. What is the best explanation?
opts: Hair cells for the highest pitches wear out first as people grow older
items.why: The hair cells for the highest pitches sit at the start of the cochlea, where every sound passes, and they wear out first over the years.

items.p: In the family pitch test, everyone stopped hearing the note at exactly 16,000 hertz, even the children. What might have gone wrong?
items.a: The phone's speaker may not be able to play notes above 16,000 hertz. Then nobody could hear, whatever their age. We could try a different speaker.
items.why: A strong answer suspects the equipment when everyone gets the same result. That is good scientific thinking.

items.p: Walls and doors block high sounds more than low sounds.
items.why: True. That is why you hear the drum beat of a neighbour's music but not the words. In the door test, the high note usually dropped more.

items.p: Match each animal to their hearing and how it helps.
pairs: hears echoes of their own ultrasound calls to find insects
hears bat calls and dives away
hears low rumbles from herd members far away
hears the very high squeaks of mice
hears with ears on her front legs
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal hears the sounds their life depends on.

items.p: Sound has reached the cochlea. Put what happens next in order.
items: the brain makes the sound you hear
the hair cells send signals along the nerve
the tufts on the hair cells bend
a: the tufts on the hair cells bend
the hair cells send signals along the nerve
the brain makes the sound you hear
items.why: The ripple bends the tufts, the bending makes the signal, and the nerve carries it to the brain.

items.p: Rekha's grandfather keeps the TV very loud. The family argues about what to do.

views.says: We should all just talk louder to Thatha. Shouting is the easiest fix.
Shouting makes it harder. We should face him, turn off the fan and get his hearing tested.
I hear the newsreader fine. I just miss your voices.

items.ask: Pick one view and support it with what you know about high sounds and hearing loss. Then answer back from one other view.
items.a: A strong answer says Thatha probably hears low voices but not high ones, so he hears the deep newsreader but misses children's higher voices. It supports the mother: shouting makes voices higher and blurs them, while facing him and cutting noise helps, and an audiologist can test him. It gives Rekha credit for wanting to help quickly.
items.why: Each person sees part of it. Thatha's own words are the best clue.

items.p: Why does your recorded voice sound strange to you?
opts: You normally hear yourself through the bones of your head too, which adds low sounds
Your voice is different in the morning
items.why: Other people hear only the air part of your voice. You also hear the bone part, which carries low sounds well. So you sound deeper to yourself than you really do to others.

items.p: Draw the band of pitches, from very low to very high. Show where people hear, and put an elephant, a dog and a bat where they belong.
items.a: A long strip with people in the middle, the elephant reaching below the people's band, the dog reaching a bit above it, and the bat far above it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that people hear only the middle of a much bigger band.
items.art: A long empty strip labelled 'low' at one end and 'high' at the other.

items.p: 1 ____ means one vibration in one second.
items.why: Hertz counts vibrations each second. A tone of 1,000 hertz vibrates 1,000 times every second.

items.p: Sort these sounds: can most people hear them or not?
cats: Too high or too low for people
items: Too high or too low for people
the lowest part of an elephant's rumble
Too high or too low for people
Too high or too low for people
items.a: see items
items.why: Dog whistles and bat calls are ultrasound. The lowest part of an elephant's rumble is infrasound. The others are in the middle band people hear.

items.p: A mixer grinder fails the arm's-length test. Give two ways to protect your ears without stopping the cooking.
items.a: Shut the kitchen door and go to another room while it runs. Or keep it running only as long as needed.
items.why: A strong answer uses distance, a barrier or less time.

items.p: After a loud firecracker, your ears ring for a while. This is a sign the hair cells were hurt.
items.why: True. Ringing and muffled hearing after loud sound mean hair cells were stressed. It usually gets better in a day, but if it happens again and again, the harm adds up.

items.p: Why might low rumbles be useful to an elephant herd spread across a forest?
opts: Low sounds travel far and pass through trees
Low sounds are quieter, so tigers won't hear
items.why: Low sounds lose less on the way and get past trees and leaves better than high ones. So herd members far apart can stay in touch. Elephants do trumpet with high sounds too.

items.p: Which of these does NOT hear ultrasound?
items.why: People cannot hear sounds above about 20,000 hertz. Bats, dogs and mice can.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out if a woollen cap blocks more sound than a cotton scarf. Say what you keep the same and what you change.
items.a: Use the volume test. Keep the same phone, song, distance, room and listener. Change only the cover: cap or scarf. Turn the volume up the same way, try each twice, and compare the steps.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing and keeps everything else the same, and repeats the test.

items.p: Two scientists argue about a forest at night, full of bat calls.

views.says: The forest is noisy. My microphone shows it is full of sound.
The forest is quiet. I can't hear a thing.

items.ask: Who is right? Use what you found at step 1 of the volume test. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer says both are describing something real. The air is full of vibration, as the microphone shows, but it is too high for human ears, so for the woman it is quiet. It might say the forest is noisy for a bat and quiet for a person.
items.why: There is no single answer. Whether a place is 'quiet' depends on who is listening.

items.p: Birds can grow new hair cells but people cannot. If scientists learn how birds do it, how might that help people?
items.a: It might one day help people with hearing loss grow new hair cells and hear again.
items.why: A strong answer links the bird finding to people whose hair cells are broken.

items.p: In the door test, Sneha scored the low note 2 with the door open and 2 with it shut. She scored the high note 3 open and 1 shut. What do her results show?
opts: The door blocked the high note more
The door blocked the low note more
items.why: The low note did not drop at all. The high note dropped by 2. So the door blocked the high note more.

items.p: In 1794, Louis Jurine plugged bats' ears with wax and they bumped into walls. Why didn't this prove that bats make sounds?
items.a: It showed bats need their ears, but nobody could hear any sound from them. They might have been listening to other sounds. It took a machine that picks up ultrasound, in 1938, to show the bats were calling.
items.why: A strong answer sees that an experiment can show one thing without proving the next.

items.p: Draw an audiogram for a grandmother who hears low sounds well but high sounds poorly. Put dots from low pitch on the left to high pitch on the right.
items.a: Dots high up on the left, near the normal line, dropping lower towards the right.
items.why: On an audiogram, a lower dot means the sound had to be louder to be heard. High-pitch loss shows as dots falling on the right.
items.art: An empty chart with 'low pitch' to 'high pitch' along the bottom and 'soft' at the top to 'loud' at the bottom.

items.p: A barn owl hunts mice in the dark. Her two ear openings are at different heights on her head. How does that help?
opts: She can tell if a sound is above or below her, as well as left or right
items.why: A sound reaches the two ears a little differently. With one ear higher, the owl can work out up and down as well as left and right, and pounce on a mouse under leaves.

items.p: If both your eardrums were damaged, you could still hear a little through the bones of your head.
items.why: True. Bone conduction carries vibrations straight to the cochlea. Some hearing aids work this way, by vibrating the bone behind the ear.

items.p: Your voice sounds deeper to you than to your friends. Which one is your 'real' voice? Give reasons for your answer.
items.a: Any answer with reasons. For example: the recording is how others hear me, so it is my voice in the air. Or: both are real, one through the air and one through my bones.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child heard in the recording and the humming test, and sees that both are real ways of hearing.

items.p: Put these sounds from lowest to highest pitch.
items: the lowest part of an elephant's rumble
a: the lowest part of an elephant's rumble
items.why: The elephant's rumble is infrasound. A child's voice is a few hundred hertz. A mosquito's whine is a little higher. A dog whistle is ultrasound.

items.p: Sort these: do they help someone with high-pitch hearing loss understand you?
items.a: see items
items.why: Facing and lip-reading, less background noise and slower speech help. Shouting makes the voice higher and blurrier, and covering your mouth hides your lips.

items.p: Why do the three tiny bones make the push stronger before it reaches the cochlea?
opts: The cochlea is full of liquid, which is harder to move than air
The brain needs the sound slower
The cochlea is very far away
items.why: Liquid is much harder to set moving than air. The bones collect the push from the large eardrum onto the tiny stirrup, making it strong enough to ripple the liquid.

items.p: Many moths have ears only for the high pitches that bats use. Why might a moth not need to hear low sounds?
items.a: The danger in a moth's life is bats, and bats call in high pitches. Hearing that band is what keeps the moth alive.
items.why: A strong answer links the hearing to the problem in the moth's life.

items.p: Sound too low for people to hear is called ____.
items.why: Infra means below. Infrasound is below about 20 hertz. Elephants and pigeons hear some of it.

items.p: On the picture of a cricket, label where her ears are.
a: on her front legs, just below the knee
items.why: Crickets hear with thin patches on their front legs. A strong answer marks both front legs.
items.art: An outline of a cricket from the side, with blank label lines.

items.p: Which one does NOT protect your hearing?
opts: Pressing your ear flaps shut near a horn
Turning earphones up to hear over traffic
Shutting the door on a mixer
items.why: Turning earphones up over traffic adds loud sound right at the ear. It is safer to take them out or move somewhere quieter.

applications: Hearing tests by audiologists, and newborn hearing checks in hospitals
Hearing aids, which make sounds louder for the pitches a person misses
Cochlear implants, which send electric signals straight to the auditory nerve

open_questions.q: Why can birds grow new hair cells, but people cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are studying the genes that switch this on in birds and fish. They hope one day to help people with hearing loss.

open_questions.q: Why do some people hear a ringing that never stops, called tinnitus?
open_questions.why_open: It often follows hearing loss, but nobody fully knows how the brain makes a sound that isn't there, or how to stop it.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a bat to hear echoes?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure what a bat's ears and brain do. Nobody has a way to know what the bat experiences.

open_questions.q: How do hundreds of bats calling at once in a cave not confuse each other?
open_questions.why_open: Bats seem to change their calls to avoid each other, but scientists are still working out exactly how.

maths.problem: In the volume test, Kavya heard the song at step 2 with open ears and at step 8 with her ear flaps pressed shut. How many more steps did she need with the flaps shut?
maths.explain: 8 take away 2 is 6. So pressing the flaps shut made her need 6 more steps before she heard the song.
maths.context: This is about the volume test, where you turn a phone up step by step until the listener hears it.
maths.why_maths: The step number alone doesn't say how much a cover blocks. The difference from open ears does.

maths.problem: Kavya's results: open ears 2, cupped hands 3, towel 5, ear flaps shut 8. Draw a bar chart. Which cover blocked about twice as much as the towel did?
maths.explain: The towel needed 3 more steps than open ears (5 take away 2). The flaps needed 6 more (8 take away 2). 6 is twice 3.
maths.context: This is about the volume test results.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which cover blocks most, and comparing differences tells you by how much.

maths.problem: In a family pitch test: Kavya (9) heard up to 18,000 hertz, Amma (38) up to 16,000, and Appooppan (70) up to 9,000. Put them in order and describe the pattern. Predict roughly where a 20-year-old cousin might stop.
maths.answer: Kavya, Amma, Appooppan. The older the person, the lower they stop. A 20-year-old might stop somewhere between 16,000 and 18,000 hertz.
maths.explain: The numbers go down as age goes up. A 20-year-old is between Kavya and Amma in age, so a good guess is between their numbers. Real people vary, so it is only a prediction.
maths.context: This is about the family pitch test, where a note rises until each person stops hearing it.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order reveals a pattern, and a pattern lets you make a prediction you can test.

maths.problem: In the noise diary, the mixer ran for 6 minutes in the morning and 4 in the evening, every day for 5 days. How many loud minutes is that in all? If the family shuts the kitchen door each time, how many loud minutes have they protected their ears from?
maths.explain: 6 plus 4 is 10 minutes a day. 10 minutes for 5 days is 50 minutes. Shutting the door each time protects their ears for all 50.
maths.context: This is about the family noise diary, where you note every loud moment for 5 days.
maths.why_maths: Small loud moments add up over days. Multiplying shows how big a difference one simple habit makes.

maths.problem: A young child hears from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. A dog hears up to about 45,000 hertz. About how many times higher can the dog hear than the child?
maths.explain: Two lots of 20,000 is 40,000, and 45,000 is a little more. So the dog hears a little over twice as high.
maths.context: This is about animals that hear sounds too high for people.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'twice as high' gives a clearer picture of a dog's hearing than two big numbers do.

roots.context: We have been learning how the ear catches sound, how to protect it, and which sounds other animals hear. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: At the lowest volume steps, the phone was playing, yet you heard nothing. The sound reached your ears, but it was too soft for them to catch. Bats, cats and elephants catch sounds that human ears miss. So a room that seems silent to you still has sounds in it.
deep_truth.habit: We say a room is 'silent' when we hear nothing, as if no sound were there. But silent only tells us about our own ears. The same room can be full of sound for a cat, a bat or a mouse.
deep_truth.evidence: In the volume test, the phone was playing at step 1, but nobody heard it until a higher step. In the pitch test, a 20,000 hertz tone played while most people heard nothing, and a dog would hear it easily.

three.who_am_i: You are a listener with your own band of hearing. Your ears catch some sounds and miss others, and your band changes as you grow.
three.what_is_life: Every creature hears what their own life needs. A moth hears the bat, a cat hears the mouse, and an elephant hears the herd far away.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of vibrations, far more than any one creature hears. Each listener hears their own part of it.

roots.thread: One room holds one set of vibrations. A child, a grandfather, a cat and a mouse in that room each hear a different part of them. None of them hears all of it, and each hears what matters for their life. The same world shows up as many worlds of sound, one for each listener.

teachings.teaching: The teacher says there is something that is the ear of the ear and the mind of the mind. It is what hears through the ear.
teachings.link: The ear passes on vibrations, and the hair cells send signals. But something in you hears. The Upanishad asks what that listener is, a question science has not answered.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text from the Pali Canon: the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Some blind men each touch one part of an elephant. One feels the ear and says an elephant is like a winnowing basket. One feels the leg and says it is like a pillar. Each is sure he alone is right.
teachings.link: A person, a bat and an elephant each hear one band of the sounds in the same forest. Each band is real, and none is the whole.

teachings.teaching: The composer John Cage sat in a room built to block all sound. He still heard two sounds, from his own body. He wrote that there is no such thing as empty time or empty space: there is always something to hear.
teachings.link: In the volume test you found that a room can be playing sound while you hear nothing. Cage found that even the quietest room still has sound.

science.text: People hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz. Bats, mice, cats and moths hear far above that, and elephants and pigeons hear below it.
What hearing is like from the inside, for a person or a bat, is still an open question for science and philosophy.

other_view.view: A sound is the experience of hearing. Vibrations nobody hears are only vibrations, not sounds. On this view, an empty forest at night has movement in the air, but no sound until someone listens.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat today. The volume test needs only a phone and a 3-metre space, and works in any quiet room. The fan must be off, or the open-ears step rises. On some phones the lowest volume step is already audible at 3 metres, so the step says to move further away or into the next room if the listener hears step 1. Ear covers never go inside the ear: the 'flaps shut' cover is the small cartilage flap pressed over the ear hole. The pitch test uses a free browser tone generator at a moderate volume set at 1,000 hertz, without earphones. Phone speakers often can't play above about 16,000 to 18,000 hertz, so the step tells parents to try a laptop if everyone stops at the same number. The door test compares how much each note drops, because low notes sound softer to us at the same volume. Ear popping uses swallowing with the nose pinched, never blowing. Foam earplugs are kept away from children under 5. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1793, in Italy, Lazzaro Spallanzani wondered how bats fly at night without hitting anything. He covered the eyes of some bats, and they still flew around his room easily. In 1794 a Swiss surgeon, Louis Jurine, tried plugging bats' ears with wax instead. Now the bats bumped into walls. Spallanzani repeated the test and found the same. So hearing mattered. But nobody could hear any sound from the bats. The famous French scientist Georges Cuvier said bats must feel the air with the skin of their wings, by touch. Most people accepted that for more than a hundred years. Then in 1938, in America, a student named Donald Griffin brought bats to the physicist George Pierce. Pierce had built a machine that could pick up sounds too high for people to hear. When the bats flew in front of it, the machine was full of their calls. Bats call in ultrasound and listen to the echoes. Griffin later named this echolocation. The wrong idea came from one mistake: people thought that a sound they could not hear did not exist.
how_we_found_out.who: Lazzaro Spallanzani in Italy, Louis Jurine in Switzerland, Georges Cuvier in France, and Donald Griffin and George Pierce in America
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Bats find their way by touch, feeling the air with their wings. Jurine's wax plugs showed that bats need their ears. Pierce's machine showed that bats make sounds too high for people to hear, and use the echoes to find their way.
